analysis.title: Oil is squeezing, AI is splitting and volatility is asleep
key_insights: JPMorgan: the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East to China has risen to about $35 per barrel from about $3 earlier this year, putting delivered Middle Eastern crude at about $143 per barrel for Chinese buyers.

The April oil problem was a physical shortage. The current squeeze is about the cost of moving oil. Energy importers face a larger cost shock than benchmark crude suggests, and European refining margins are under pressure.

Oil implied volatility is depressed even as oil approaches recent highs. The crowd is focused on downside risk and prices little upside volatility. The Market Ear sees cheap upside optionality as a way to position for a squeeze.

Nomura: SPX 10-day realized volatility is 7 and three-month implied volatility is at the 2nd percentile of its one-year range. Heavy short-dated volatility selling gives dealers gamma, which dampens intraday moves and reinforces low volatility.

The volatility-selling loop is self-reinforcing: low realized volatility encourages more selling, which keeps realized volatility low. The risk is what happens if those flows reverse. The Market Ear agrees with Nomura's logic and says the missing ingredient for a compelling long-vol setup is quants recommending selling options at these levels.
SpotGamma: the weekly straddle is at a very long-term low. Cheap volatility can be used without being bearish.

The correlation between the S&P 500 and upside call volatility has risen toward +0.5, a reversal from the normally negative relationship. Nomura: SPX call skew is at the 99.6th percentile of its one-year range while demand for downside protection is subdued.

Goldman: aggressive call demand and very low hedge-fund net exposure show investors worried about missing the next leg higher. The next volatility shock could come from investors chasing stocks higher.
Investors are paying for an abrupt volatility spike but are reluctant to hedge a conventional equity selloff (GS).

KOSPI and Taiwan have diverged sharply. Korea is a leveraged bet on the memory cycle, while Taiwan is dominated by TSMC and advanced manufacturing. The market is questioning memory profit sustainability and still rewarding AI infrastructure.

JPMorgan: Nvidia's projected cash flow gains exceed 100% of the expected decline in hyperscaler free cash flow. JPMorgan still sees attractive returns on certain data-center investments, but there is a timing mismatch.
The KOSPI vs SOX divergence keeps widening, with Korea pricing peak memory earnings and US semis trading the structural AI growth story. The Market Ear doubts such an extreme divergence can persist.

KOSPI and semiconductor volatility have compressed from previous highs, which may offer cheaper entry points for hedges or directional option views, with dispersion between winners and losers likely to widen.

sector_views.rationale: Korea memory is pricing peak earnings while Taiwan and US semis trade the structural AI story. The Market Ear expects the divergence to be hard to sustain.
Oil is approaching recent highs with depressed implied volatility, and shipping costs are adding to delivered crude prices.

tension_points.bull_case: Heavy short-dated volatility selling supplies dealers with gamma and dampens moves, keeping realized volatility at 7 and implied volatility at the 2nd percentile.
tension_points.bear_case: If the flows suppressing volatility reverse, volatility could spike. Extreme call skew and call-volatility correlation suggest a shock could come from investors chasing stocks higher.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reversal of the short-dated volatility selling flows.

tension_points.bear_case: Korea may be the first market to recognize that AI boom economics are getting more complicated, and cracks in one corner could spread.
